newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish police go on trial in murder case.
newsitem.headline: Turkish police go on trial in murder case.

text.p: Turkish police beat suspects until their wooden batons broke, a witness on Friday told the opening of a murder trial that one rights activist dismissed as "a comedy of justice".
Journalist Aydin Aydemir said she saw police clubbing people in an Istanbul sports complex where fellow reporter Metin Goktepe was allegedly battered to death by police in January.
"We heard sounds of beating and wooden sticks breaking. I didn't see Metin but I saw a lot of people being beaten. I thought the death toll would have been greater," she said.
Forty-eight policemen went on trial in the southwestern town of Aydin for Goktepe's death in a trial being held under the critical eye of Turkey's Western allies and rights workers.

In another major case, an appeals court confirmed a 20-month suspended sentence against Yasar Kemal, Turkey's best-known living author, for promoting separatism in an article calling for a political solution to Kurdish demands for autonomy.

"This can occur only in a closed system. My article calls on peace, seeks ways of ending the prolonged bloody war and I am found guilty for provoking separatism. Can you believe it?" Kemal told Reuters from his home in Istanbul.
Another journalist, Murat Inceoglu of the liberal daily Yeni Yuzyil, told the Aydin court he last saw Goktepe as he disappeared behind a line of riot police.
"You talk too much. I am taking you into custody," he quoted a policeman as telling Goktepe.

Claims of extrajudicial killings and deaths by torture in Turkish police custody are rife -- the Ankara-based Human Rights Association says there were 21 just in August this year -- but it is rare that the perpetrators come before the law.
Aydemir said police rounded up scores of people at random for an identity check in Eyup sports complex after the funerals of two far-left militant prisoner.
"It was like a concentration camp. There were old and young people. Some were picked up while going to the grocers or trying to catch a bus," she told the packed court.

The trial was transferred to Aydin from Istanbul, some 800 km (500 miles) away, a move rights activists say was an attempt to keep the court proceedings out of the public eye. Authorities have cited unspecified "secuarity concerns" for the decision.

"What we saw today was a comedy of justice. It damages justice to a great degree to have a court case (so far) from where the incident took place," Robert Menard, of press group Reporters sans Frontiers, told journalists outside the court.
Nonetheless about 300 relatives, journalists and observers turned up at the court on Friday morning, forcing judge Turgut Yildirim to switch the trial to a sports hall.
Yildirim later adjourned the case until November 29, after rejecting appeals from the Goktepe family that the accused policemen be taken into custody pending resolution of the case.
The officers were not in court and have been allowed to answer the accusations to other court officials without travelling to Aydin. No formal plea is needed under Turkish law.

"This is a case important for the victim, of course, and also for Turkey," Euro MP Magda Aelvoet from Belgium told Reuters at the court. "Turkey might show with a correct trial that it is serious about respecting law," she said.
Euro MPs have threatened to block hundreds of millions of dollars in European Union aid to Turkey, partly because of Ankara's human rights problems.
Rights group Amnesty International this month launched a worldwide campaign to focus attention on abuses in Turkey, particularly extrajudicial killings, torture and disappearances.
Turkey says Amnesty is biased against it, but Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller has vowed to clamp down on rights abuses. Turkish media has given rare prominence to Goktepe's killing.
"They killed my son," Goktepe mother Fadime, 65, told the court referring to the police. Relatives wore tee-shirts with a photograph of the dead journalist printed on them.
